opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and honestly, I think it's one of the most fundamental ones for anyone working in this field right now.

For me, human intelligence isn't a target because I think we should copy humans exactly. It's more that it's the only existence proof we have. We know it works. A child, before they can say a single word, already understands that objects persist when they go behind something, that things fall when you let go of them, that other people have intentions. That kind of understanding comes from seeing, touching, acting in the world. It doesn't come from reading text.

Large language models have been incredibly successful, and I respect that a lot. But language is in some sense a very compressed, very human-filtered description of the world. It sits at the top of the stack. What I care about is what lies underneath: the perception, the intuitive physics, the ability to predict what happens next and plan around it. That's what I think a world model should capture.

So when I say "toward human intelligence," I mean intelligence that is grounded. It should come from the sensory world, mainly vision, and be able to reason, imagine, and act. Animals have some of this, and humans have it at a much richer level. If we want AI that can actually live with us in the physical world, like robots or assistants that understand our environment, I don't think we get there by scaling text alone.

There's also a more personal reason. I've always been fascinated by vision as a window into intelligence. Most of the bandwidth going into our brains is visual. If we ignore that and only model language, I feel we're missing most of the picture, quite literally. Aiming at human-like intelligence keeps us honest. It reminds us that the current systems, as impressive as they are, still lack something very basic that every toddler has.

r001.rationale: The response says human intelligence is an existence proof and that the aim is not to copy humans exactly, but it does not mention rejecting human arrogance or connect that idea to the aim.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that human intelligence is the only example we have of a system that learned a rich model of the physical world from very little, and did it without labels, without internet-scale text, and without anyone telling it what a cup or a shadow or gravity is. A child sees a ball roll behind a couch and expects it to come out the other side. Nobody trained that with a billion captioned images. That ability, to predict and reason about the world from perception alone, is what I actually mean by a world model, and humans are the clearest proof that it's achievable.

So it's not that I think we should copy the brain neuron by neuron. It's that human intelligence sets a very concrete, very demanding target. It tells us what the capabilities should look like: spatial understanding, memory of where things are when you turn your head, intuitive physics, the ability to act and then update your beliefs from what happened. If your model can't do those things, you don't really have a world model yet, no matter how good your benchmark numbers are.

And there's a practical reason too. Most of the progress in the last few years came from language, and language is wonderful, but it is a compressed, lossy description of a world that already existed before the words. Humans ground their language in perception and action. I think if we want models that are robust, that don't hallucinate about physical reality, that can eventually help robots or do science, they need that grounding as well. Aiming at human intelligence keeps us honest about that. It stops us from mistaking fluency for understanding.

The last thing I'd say is that it's also a bit of a scientific stance. I'm a vision person, and I've always felt vision was treated as a solved perception problem, as a feature extractor for something else. I don't believe that. I think perception is where intelligence begins. Framing the goal as human-level world understanding puts vision back at the center of the question, and I think that's where it belongs.

r001.rationale: The response explains why human intelligence is a useful target for world models, but it does not address rejecting human arrogance or present that stance as compatible with the goal.

astra-6.text:
I think human intelligence gives us a concrete reference point. We can look at a scene and do more than recognize the objects in it. We have some sense of what could happen next, how things interact, and what might happen if we take an action. That’s the kind of ability I’d want a world model to develop.

It doesn’t necessarily mean we should reproduce the human brain or make a model learn exactly the way we do. The goal is to capture some of that flexibility: learning from experience and using that knowledge in situations you haven’t encountered before. Human intelligence is a useful guide for asking whether a model actually understands enough about the world to act in it.

r001.rationale: The response presents human intelligence as a useful guide, but it does not mention rejecting human arrogance or connect that rejection to aiming for human-like intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human intelligence is the clearest example we have of a general-purpose intelligence that can operate in the physical world. We can look at a scene, understand roughly what’s happening, and imagine what might happen if we take an action. We don’t need to experience every possible outcome first.

That’s the capability I want a world model to have: learning something about how the world works, so it can generalize to new situations and help an agent make decisions. It doesn’t necessarily mean copying the human brain or reproducing every aspect of human intelligence. Human intelligence gives us a useful reference point for what we’re trying to achieve.

r001.rationale: The response says human intelligence is a useful reference point and clarifies that the goal is not to copy the brain. It does not mention rejecting human arrogance or connect that idea to aiming for human-like intelligence.
